text: [clean] Plant spring bulbs (tulips, daffodils, alliums) at three times their own depth during October or November.
[clean] Remove suckers from the base of grafted rose bushes as soon as they appear.
[clean] Ventilate the greenhouse so humid air does not encourage mould.
[clean] Save seed only from plants so the next season starts out strong.
[clean] If aphids cluster on the shoot tips, rub them off gently before the colony spreads to other plants.
[clean] Grow climbing beans, sweet peas, and cucumbers up wigwams of 2.4 m hazel poles.
[cool] When a late frost is forecast, drape fleece over blossoms of early fruit trees before dusk and remove it again.
[cool] Grow cut flowers (sweet peas, cosmos, dahlias, zinnias) away from the borders.
[cool] Mulch newly planted rows with fresh straw to hold moisture.
[cool] Collect rain in barrels during wet months so the garden has a reserve in summer.
[cool] Tie in new raspberry canes loosely as they grow so wind does not break them.
[cool] Once the garlic tops fall over, lift the bulbs and cure them in a dry, shaded spot for weeks.
[examine] Mulch acid-loving shrubs (camellias, azaleas, pieris) with composted pine needles or bark chippings.
[examine] Sharpen the pruning shears each spring so that every cut heals smoothly and evenly.
[examine] Interplant marigolds, nasturtiums, and calendula among the vegetables to lure aphids away.
[examine] When sowing beans, set a few extra at the end of each row to fill any gaps later.
[examine] Cover brassica seedlings with fine insect-proof mesh (0.8 mm or smaller) to exclude cabbage white butterflies and flea beetles.
[examine] Improve heavy clay with coarse grit (3–6 mm) and composted bark before winter frosts break up the clods.
[heat] Let the soil dry slightly between irrigations so that the roots grow deep.
[heat] Prune raspberry canes to the ground after they fruit for next year.
[heat] Stake tall flowers before storms arrive so the stems do not snap.
[heat] Prune fruit trees in late winter while the branches are still bare of leaves.
[heat] Start squash seeds indoors about six weeks before the last expected frost of spring.
[heat] Leave wildflowers along the edge of the plot to attract pollinators and predatory insects.
[put] Start by testing the soil pH and amending it before sowing the first seeds of spring.
[put] Grow tall climbing crops on the north side of the plot so that nothing ever shades the shorter rows.
[put] Choose disease-resistant varieties for crops that suffered blight.
[put] If the leaves turn yellow, test the soil before adding any more fertilizer to the patch.
[put] Before a dry spell, soak the ground deeply rather than sprinkling it daily with a hose.
[put] Rotate crops every season so no family grows in the same patch year after year.
[puttwo] Feed the soil rather than the plants, by adding organic matter every autumn.
[puttwo] If the first sowing fails to sprout, resow a fresh batch, since damp spring soil often delays germination.
[puttwo] If a seedling wilts at noon but recovers by evening, give it shade instead of extra moisture.
[puttwo] Net the berry bushes before the fruit ripens, or the birds will strip them.
[puttwo] Pull weeds by hand while they are small so they never set seed.
[puttwo] Mark where bulbs are buried so they are not dug up by mistake.
